newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai Airways strike paralyses cargo movement.
newsitem.headline: Thai Airways strike paralyses cargo movement.

text.p: Nearly 1,500 air cargo workers of Thai Airways International Plc continued their strike for the second day on Tuesday, paralysing cargo shipments at dozens of airlines in Bangkok's busy Don Muang airport.
Airline industry sources told Reuters the industrial action stranded several hundred tonnes of cargo, mostly electronics and textile goods, at the international airport.
Around 1,000 strikers also rallied in front of Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's office against the government's October 15 decision to launch a new Thai air cargo carrier.

Workers fear the introduction of the carrier, Thai Air Cargo Co Ltd, could affect their jobs. Strike leaders have asked for a government guarantee protecting job benefits and welfare of air cargo workers when the new airline is introduced.
Airlines hit by the strike were mostly Asian, including Cathay Pacific Airways, Singapore Airlines, China Airlines and Malaysian Airlines
Cathay Pacific is still operating its regular seven daily flights through Bangkok. A clerk at Singapore Airlines, however, said four of its five daily flights would be affected by the strike action.
Both Cathay and Singapore flights are passenger flights with attached cargo. Cathay for example typically carries 30-40 tonnes of cargo on its flights.
A staffer at All Nippon Airways, which flies 12 passenger and five cargo flights a week to Bangkok, said the firm was suffering heavily because of the dispute.
Up to 70 percent of the airport's cargo is handled by employees of Thai Airways, which is 93 percent owned by the Thai government.
Most European and American airlines were unaffected. Their cargo is handled by separate workers belonging to the Airport Authority of Thailand (AAT), which runs the airport.
But airline employees said striking workers refused to unlock a warehouse to allow AAT staff to handle stranded cargo.

The striking workers said the government's decision to create the new airline was not transparent and alleged some politicians had pushed to form the carrier, which will be 40 percent owned by Thai Airways.
They also questioned the government's motive in allowing private interests into the lucrative air cargo business.

A cabinet spokesman told reporters a senior transport and communications ministry official was assigned to hold talks with striking workers, but did not elaborate. He said the cabinet may consider the issue next Tuesday.
Thai Airways' shares ended up 0.50 baht at 44.50 baht ($1.75) despite news of the strike.

Saengchai Ekapatpanich, a spokesman for the electronics and electrical appliances group of the Federation of Thai Industries, said the strike had hurt over 100 electronic manufacturers waiting for imported parts.

"This is a dispute between the government and employees of a state enterprise and the private sector should not be made to suffer. The delay in getting imported parts would make it hard to meet our shipment schedules," he said.
Saengchai said the strike was ill-timed because it took place while Thailand was struggling to revive sluggish exports. He said government leaders should act quickly to help exporters.
